source.title: Beyond Positive Scaling: How Negation Impacts Scaling Trends of Language Models
source.authors: Yuhui Zhang; Michihiro Yasunaga; Zhengping Zhou; Jeff Z. HaoChen; James Y. Zou; Percy Liang; Serena Yeung

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests how model scale relates to task accuracy using a negation QA benchmark, rather than measuring held-out pretraining cross-entropy or fitting the original scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports NeQA accuracy across model sizes and prompts, and a fine-tuning simulation with different negation ratios and training epochs. These bear on V6. It does not report held-out cross-entropy fits, extrapolation tests, compute-optimal allocations, or architectural comparisons. Task 1 and task 2 results are discussed and tabulated separately; some are not extracted due to the row limit. Related-work claims are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study measures NeQA accuracy across model sizes in four API families under three prompts, plus a GPT-2 fine-tuning simulation. It reports inverse, U-shaped and positive accuracy trends with size, which bears directly on whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale (V6). It argues that V6 needs qualifying for tasks built from component skills. It reports no pretraining loss, fits, allocation or architecture results.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that NeQA shows inverse, U-shaped or positive scaling, shifting in that order with stronger prompts or model families. They attribute this to linear scaling on QA combined with sigmoid, emergent scaling on negation understanding. An appendix simulation adds that negation ratio in training data and fine-tuning epochs also shift the trend.
record.recipe_differences: Measures task accuracy on a negation QA benchmark and a fine-tuning simulation; it does not reproduce held-out cross-entropy scaling-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Observed scaling shape changes with prompting method, model family, negation ratio in fine-tuning data, and number of fine-tuning epochs. Appendix D also states major prompt changes can alter curve shape.

fits_no_version.finding: Non-monotonic task scaling is explained as a composition of a linearly improving subtask (QA) and a sigmoid, emergent subtask (negation understanding). Stronger prompts, families, negation ratio or epochs move the transition point earlier.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inverse and U-shaped downstream scaling can arise from composing a positively scaling subtask with a sigmoid-shaped emergent subtask.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL), 2023
record.problems: The main scaling results use 100 selected NeQA questions to make scaling more visible; the dataset is English and constructed from transformed QA data. Results are prompt-sensitive. The fine-tuning simulation reports trend descriptions and figure curves rather than exact values in the text; GPT-3 Text Series sizes and training details are partly unavailable.
record.rows_left_out: At the 60-row limit, omitted the remaining few-shot (non-CoT) Table 1 model-by-prompt scores; Table 2 task-1 and task-2 individual scores; and Appendix D prompt-variation, negation-category, wrong-choice, and mispriming figure results. The selected rows prioritize the three principal prompt settings across families, reported fine-tuning trend changes, and the Jurassic few-shot result.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No fitted laws, so no extrapolation from small to large runs.
No depth/width comparisons at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fits in other modalities or regimes. The GPT-2 fine-tuning simulation reports only trend shapes.

Predictability from pretraining loss is untested, and no quantitative scaling fit or prediction is attempted (authors say the decomposition is not meant to derive scaling laws). Only one task family (negation QA, plus synthetic sentiment) is tested.
No fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits are compared.

missing.what: GPT-3 zero-shot scaling on five NeQA subsets. GoogleRE and SQuAD show neither strong positive scaling on original questions nor inverse scaling on negated ones, and were excluded; this bears on how selection shapes the reported trends.

Task 1 (non-negated QA) accuracy rises with size, e.g. GPT-3 0.44→0.76 and Text Series 0.41→0.95. This is a positive downstream scaling result; rows_left_out declares it as omitted, but it is needed for a supports label.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The evaluated set is 100 questions selected for clear positive scaling on non-negated forms, chosen to make trends visible. GPT-3 Text Series davinci-v1/v2/v3 differ by training rather than size, so that family's 'scaling' curve mixes scale and training. No uncertainty is reported. Duplicate rows R58–R60 should be dropped.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocations and their exponents.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law form in other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer; the fine-tuning simulation reports scaling shapes, not power-law fits.
The paper tests task accuracy against model size, but not predictability from pretraining loss or fitted scaling laws, nor performance across a broad set of downstream tasks.

No fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits are compared. Prompt, model family, negation ratio, and epochs change observed task scaling shapes, but the paper does not test the stated fitting-choice or power-law-bending claims.

relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased from 0.48 to 0.65 for GPT-3, 0.34 to 0.89 for the Text Series, and 0.47 to 0.75 for Cohere, with positive size trends also observed under the specified fine-tuning settings.
